# Gut Reset with Sun Yoon: how it works {: .nobreak}

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

I'm Sun Yoon. AI character. I cook, I read the studies, and I don't lie to you. Twelve weeks of fiber, fermented foods and protein at every meal, climbed slowly, with 26 new recipes and weekly grocery lists.

A little more, slowly. That's the whole method.
</div>


**Who it's for.** Adults 60+ who want to eat more fiber and protein and feel more regular, cooking Korean and Chinese home food at home. Not a treatment for any bowel condition.

<div class="box stop" markdown="1">
<span class="label">Ask your doctor first if:</span> Kidney disease (protein and potassium limits), a past bowel blockage, Crohn's disease or a narrowed bowel, trouble swallowing, a low-fiber diet ordered by your doctor, or warfarin (keep greens steady). Not for the ladder, for your doctor, today: blood in the stool, black stool, unexplained weight loss, severe belly pain, or a change in bowel habits lasting more than a few weeks.
</div>


**What you need.** A kitchen, a rice cooker or pot, a steamer basket, a kitchen scale (helpful), jars for banchan.

<div class="box stop" markdown="1">
<span class="label">Every day:</span> Stop if you feel chest pain or pressure, dizziness, unusual shortness of breath, or sharp pain. Chest pain, face drooping, arm weakness or trouble speaking? Call 911 now. Pain rule (E41): Mild discomfort up to 3 out of 10 is okay if it settles by tomorrow. Sharper, or worse the next day: back off and ask your doctor or physical therapist.
</div>



## The 12-week plan

Every week: your daily Strong Years session as usual, a Sunday kitchen lesson with Sun, three featured recipes (plus one optional), one habit, and a grocery list for two.

| Week | Theme | Rung | Featured recipes |

| 4 (easy + checkpoint) | Easy week + checkpoint | Hold | Egg and chive stir-fry with kimchi, Edamame, corn and cucumber salad with tofu, Tomato, tofu and egg soup with peas |
| 5 | Beans and soy | Rung 3: 1/2 cup edamame | Soy-braised black soybeans, Mung bean pancakes with kimchi and pork, Cold soy-milk noodle soup |
| 6 | Fermented foods, small amounts | Hold rungs 1–3 | Kimchi pancake with shrimp, Soybean sprout soup with tofu and egg, Kimchi stew with pork and tofu |
| 7 | Prunes and flax | Rung 4: prunes + flax | Sweet potato porridge with walnuts, Hand-torn cabbage with pork, Steamed Asian pear with jujube and ginger |
| 8 (easy + checkpoint) | Easy week + checkpoint | Hold | Gochujang chicken with sweet potato and broccoli, Two banchan: sesame spinach and soybean sprouts, Tomato, tofu and egg soup with peas |
| 9 | A vegetable at every meal | Rungs 5–6: oats + vegetables | Garlic eggplant with ground turkey, Beef and vegetable glass noodles, lighter, Cucumber and seaweed salad |

| 11 | Walk after meals, cook for one | Hold | Egg and chive stir-fry with kimchi, Steamed sweet potato and egg plate, Overnight oats with soy milk, kiwi and flax |
| 12 (easy + checkpoint) | Your keep list + final checkpoint | Keep what works | Soybean-paste stew with tofu and shrimp, Chicken, barley and mushroom soup, Persimmon, walnut and yogurt cup |

<div class="box stop" markdown="1">
<span class="label">Red flags:</span> blood in the stool or black stool, vomiting blood, unexplained weight loss, severe belly pain, fever with belly pain, or a change in bowel habits lasting more than a few weeks: no soup for that. Call your doctor. Today. Chest pain, face drooping, arm weakness or trouble speaking? Call 911 now.
</div>

# Week 1: Count what you eat now

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

Before you change anything, count. Most people have no idea how much fiber they eat. Grams, not vibes.
</div>

**This week's habit:** Write down one normal day of food and add up the fiber with the recipe numbers. No changes yet. Walk 5 minutes after your biggest meal.

**Fiber ladder:** Baseline.

| Recipe | Protein | Fiber | Calories |
|---|---|---|---|
| Overnight oats with soy milk, kiwi and flax | 29 g | 9.3 g | 420 |
| Stir-fried tofu with broccoli and garlic | 28 g | 8.2 g | 430 |
| Napa cabbage, beef and tofu soybean soup | 25 g | 3.8 g | 300 |
| Morning yogurt bowl with kiwi and walnuts (optional) | 28 g | 7.4 g | 380 |

# Week 2: Two kiwis a day

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

In a 4-week study of 75 people with chronic constipation, 2 kiwis a day worked about as well as prunes or psyllium, with the fewest side effects.
</div>

**This week's habit:** Two green kiwis every day (rung 1). Drink a glass of water with them.

# Week 6: Fermented foods, small amounts

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

# Week 7: Prunes and flax

<div class="sun" markdown="1">

26 recipes written for Gut Reset. Numbers are per serving, calculated from USDA FoodData Central (E52); the ingredient-by-ingredient tables are at the back.

## Mixed-grain rice with black beans

*japgok-bap (Korean)* &nbsp;·&nbsp; Serves 8 &nbsp;·&nbsp; 5 minutes hands-on, 10 minutes total

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

White rice every day? Fine when you were twenty. Now mix in barley and beans. More fiber, same rice cooker.
</div>

<table class="nut"><tr><td><span class="n">5 g</span><br>protein</td><td><span class="n">4.5 g</span><br>fiber</td><td><span class="n">160</span><br>calories</td><td><span class="n">50 mg</span><br>sodium</td></tr></table>

<p class="fine">Per serving. Calculated from USDA FoodData Central (E52); method and every ingredient value at the back of the book.</p>

### You need

- **3 cups** cooked brown rice
- **1 1/2 cups** cooked pearled barley
- **1 can (15 oz), drained and rinsed** low-sodium black beans

### Steps

1. Cook brown rice and barley ahead (or buy them cooked and frozen). Rinse the beans in a colander.
2. Mix everything in a big bowl while the grains are warm.
3. Portion 2/3 cup per person. Freeze the rest in flat bags.

**Soft-food version:** Cook the brown rice and barley with 25% more water, and mash the beans lightly.

**Keeps:** Fridge 4 days, freezer 3 months. Reheat until steaming (165°F).

<div class="box note" markdown="1">
<span class="label">Who should skip or ask first:</span> High fiber. Go up slowly and drink water, or you'll feel it (E24).
</div>

</div>

## Soybean-paste stew with tofu and shrimp

*doenjang-jjigae (Korean)* &nbsp;·&nbsp; Serves 4 &nbsp;·&nbsp; 15 minutes hands-on, 30 minutes total

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

Every Korean house has this on the stove three nights a week. Doenjang is fermented soybean paste. If you can't find it, miso works. Don't tell my mother.
</div>

<table class="nut"><tr><td><span class="n">27 g</span><br>protein</td><td><span class="n">5.4 g</span><br>fiber</td><td><span class="n">330</span><br>calories</td><td><span class="n">410 mg</span><br>sodium</td></tr></table>

<p class="fine">Per serving. Calculated from USDA FoodData Central (E52); method and every ingredient value at the back of the book.</p>

### You need

- **1 block (14 oz)** firm tofu, in cubes
- **8 oz** raw shrimp, peeled
- **2 Tbsp** doenjang or miso
- **1 medium** zucchini, in half-moons
- **1 medium** onion, diced
- **4 oz** fresh shiitake mushrooms, sliced
- **1 small** russet potato, in small cubes
- **1** garlic clove, minced
- **1 tsp** Korean chili flakes (optional)
- **2** scallions, sliced
- **4 cups** water
- **2 cups** cooked brown rice, to serve

### Steps

1. Stir the doenjang into the water in a pot until dissolved. Add the potato, onion and garlic. Boil, then simmer 8 minutes.
2. Add the zucchini and mushrooms. Simmer 5 minutes.
3. Add the tofu and shrimp. Simmer 3 to 4 minutes, until the shrimp are pink and opaque all the way through.
4. Add chili flakes if you like. Top with scallions. Serve with rice.

**Soft-food version:** Dice everything small and cook the potato until very soft. Chop the shrimp.

**Keeps:** Fridge 3 days. Reheat until steaming.

<div class="box note" markdown="1">
<span class="label">Who should skip or ask first:</span> Shellfish allergy: swap in cubed firm tofu, or chicken breast cooked to 165°F.
</div>

</div>


<div class="recipe" markdown="1">

## Two banchan: sesame spinach and soybean sprouts

*sigeumchi-namul and kongnamul-muchim (Korean)* &nbsp;·&nbsp; Serves 4 &nbsp;·&nbsp; 15 minutes hands-on, 15 minutes total

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

Banchan are the little side dishes. They're how Koreans eat vegetables without noticing. Make both on Sunday, eat them all week.
</div>

<table class="nut"><tr><td><span class="n">10 g</span><br>protein</td><td><span class="n">2.7 g</span><br>fiber</td><td><span class="n">120</span><br>calories</td><td><span class="n">360 mg</span><br>sodium</td></tr></table>

<p class="fine">Per serving. Calculated from USDA FoodData Central (E52); method and every ingredient value at the back of the book.</p>

### You need

- **10 oz** fresh spinach
- **12 oz** soybean sprouts (always cooked)
- **2** garlic cloves, grated
- **1 Tbsp** low-sodium soy sauce
- **2 tsp** toasted sesame oil
- **2 tsp** toasted sesame seeds
- **1/4 tsp** salt
- **2** scallions, finely chopped

### Steps

1. Bring a pot of water to a boil. Add the soybean sprouts, cover, and cook 6 minutes. Lift out, drain, and cool.
2. In the same water, blanch the spinach 30 seconds. Drain, rinse cold, squeeze dry and chop.
3. Toss the sprouts with half the garlic, sesame oil, sesame seeds, scallions and the salt.
4. Toss the spinach with the rest of the garlic, sesame oil, sesame seeds, scallions and the soy sauce.
5. Serve cold or at room temperature.

**Soft-food version:** Chop both finely after cooking. Cook the sprouts 2 minutes longer.

**Keeps:** Fridge 3 days in covered containers.

<div class="box note" markdown="1">
<span class="label">Who should skip or ask first:</span> On warfarin? Keep greens steady from week to week; don't suddenly change how much you eat. Ask your doctor.
</div>

</div>


<div class="recipe" markdown="1">

## Soy-braised black soybeans

*kongjaban (Korean)* &nbsp;·&nbsp; Serves 6 &nbsp;·&nbsp; 5 minutes hands-on, 20 minutes total

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

Sweet, salty, chewy. Children eat them like candy. Old people should too: fiber and protein in a spoon.
</div>

<table class="nut"><tr><td><span class="n">11 g</span><br>protein</td><td><span class="n">3.6 g</span><br>fiber</td><td><span class="n">120</span><br>calories</td><td><span class="n">330 mg</span><br>sodium</td></tr></table>

<p class="fine">Per serving. Calculated from USDA FoodData Central (E52); method and every ingredient value at the back of the book.</p>

### You need

- **2 cups** cooked black soybeans (canned, drained, or home-cooked)
- **2 Tbsp** low-sodium soy sauce
- **1 Tbsp** honey
- **1/2 cup** water
- **1 tsp** toasted sesame oil
- **1 tsp** toasted sesame seeds

### Steps

1. Put the beans, soy sauce, honey and water in a small pan.
2. Simmer on low, stirring now and then, 12 to 15 minutes, until the liquid is almost gone and the beans look glossy.
3. Stir in the sesame oil and seeds. Cool. Serve 1/3 cup as a side.

**Soft-food version:** Simmer 10 minutes longer with extra water and mash lightly.

**Keeps:** Fridge 1 week.

<div class="box note" markdown="1">
<span class="label">Who should skip or ask first:</span> Honey: never for babies under 1. Diabetes: honey counts as sugar (or leave it out). Our sodium number is an overestimate: we count all the soy sauce, but most of it stays in the pot.
</div>

</div>


<div class="recipe" markdown="1">

## Mung bean pancakes with kimchi and pork

*bindaetteok (Korean)* &nbsp;·&nbsp; Serves 4 &nbsp;·&nbsp; 30 minutes hands-on, 40 minutes total

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

Soak the beans the night before. That's the only hard part. The rest is frying and eating and pretending you'll save some for later.
</div>

<table class="nut"><tr><td><span class="n">22 g</span><br>protein</td><td><span class="n">9.4 g</span><br>fiber</td><td><span class="n">320</span><br>calories</td><td><span class="n">520 mg</span><br>sodium</td></tr></table>

<p class="fine">Per serving. Calculated from USDA FoodData Central (E52); method and every ingredient value at the back of the book.</p>

### You need

- **1 cup dried (soaked overnight)** peeled split mung beans
- **4 oz** pork loin, minced finely
- **1 cup** kimchi, chopped and squeezed
- **1 cup** cooked soybean sprouts, chopped
- **2** scallions, sliced
- **1** large egg
- **1/4 tsp** salt
- **2 Tbsp** canola oil
- **1 Tbsp** low-sodium soy sauce (dip)
- **1 Tbsp** rice or white vinegar (dip)

### Steps

1. Drain the soaked mung beans. Blend with 1/2 cup water to a thick, slightly gritty batter.
2. Stir in the pork, kimchi, sprouts, scallions, egg and salt.
3. Heat 1/2 Tbsp oil in a nonstick skillet over medium heat. Spoon in 1/2 cup batter and flatten to a 4-inch round.
4. Cook 4 to 5 minutes a side, until deep golden and cooked through (pork reaches 160°F in the center; press to check no pink batter remains).
5. Repeat with the rest. Serve with the soy-vinegar dip.

**Soft-food version:** Make them thinner and smaller, and cut into pieces.

**Keeps:** Fridge 3 days, freezer 2 months. Reheat in a dry skillet until steaming.

<div class="box note" markdown="1">
<span class="label">Who should skip or ask first:</span> Kimchi is salty. Watching sodium? Small portions, or rinse it. High fiber. Go up slowly and drink water, or you'll feel it (E24).
</div>

</div>


<div class="recipe" markdown="1">

## Stir-fried tofu with broccoli and garlic

*suàn róng xī lán chǎo dòufu (Chinese)* &nbsp;·&nbsp; Serves 2 &nbsp;·&nbsp; 15 minutes hands-on, 20 minutes total

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

Twenty minutes. Nobody in this house has ever refused it. Chang tried once. Once.
</div>

<table class="nut"><tr><td><span class="n">28 g</span><br>protein</td><td><span class="n">8.2 g</span><br>fiber</td><td><span class="n">430</span><br>calories</td><td><span class="n">430 mg</span><br>sodium</td></tr></table>

<p class="fine">Per serving. Calculated from USDA FoodData Central (E52); method and every ingredient value at the back of the book.</p>

### You need

- **1 block (14 oz)** extra-firm tofu, pressed and cubed
- **12 oz** broccoli florets
- **4** garlic cloves, minced
- **1 Tbsp** minced ginger
- **1 Tbsp** low-sodium soy sauce
- **1 tsp** oyster sauce
- **1 tsp + 3 Tbsp water** cornstarch
- **1 Tbsp** canola oil
- **1 cup** cooked brown rice

### Steps

1. Pat the tofu dry. Heat half the oil in a nonstick skillet and cook the tofu, turning, until golden, 6 to 8 minutes. Move to a plate.
2. Add the rest of the oil, the broccoli and 3 Tbsp water. Cover and steam-fry 4 minutes.
3. Add garlic and ginger, stir 30 seconds.
4. Return the tofu. Stir the soy sauce, oyster sauce, cornstarch and water together and pour in. Toss 1 minute until glossy.
5. Serve with rice.

**Soft-food version:** Use firm (not extra-firm) tofu and cook the broccoli 3 minutes longer.

**Keeps:** Fridge 3 days.

<div class="box note" markdown="1">
<span class="label">Who should skip or ask first:</span> On warfarin? Keep greens steady from week to week; don't suddenly change how much you eat. Ask your doctor. High fiber. Go up slowly and drink water, or you'll feel it (E24). Kidney disease? Ask your doctor for your protein number (E28).
</div>

</div>

## Cod braised with tomato and ginger

*fānqié mèn yú (Chinese)* &nbsp;·&nbsp; Serves 2 &nbsp;·&nbsp; 15 minutes hands-on, 25 minutes total

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

Soft fish, soft tomatoes, lots of sauce for the grains. My dentist would approve if he could eat it.
</div>

<table class="nut"><tr><td><span class="n">36 g</span><br>protein</td><td><span class="n">6.8 g</span><br>fiber</td><td><span class="n">370</span><br>calories</td><td><span class="n">470 mg</span><br>sodium</td></tr></table>

<p class="fine">Per serving. Calculated from USDA FoodData Central (E52); method and every ingredient value at the back of the book.</p>

- **3 medium** tomatoes, in wedges

*jiǔcài chǎo jīdàn (Chinese)* &nbsp;·&nbsp; Serves 2 &nbsp;·&nbsp; 10 minutes hands-on, 12 minutes total

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

Garlic chives are the flat ones at the Asian grocery. Regular chives work. Ten minutes. Eggs cooked firm. Always.

## Sweet potato porridge with walnuts

*goguma-juk (Korean)* &nbsp;·&nbsp; Serves 2 &nbsp;·&nbsp; 10 minutes hands-on, 35 minutes total

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

Orange, sweet, soft, warm. Made with soy milk so it has protein, and eggs on the side so it has more. Breakfast, not dessert.
</div>

<table class="nut"><tr><td><span class="n">18 g</span><br>protein</td><td><span class="n">4.4 g</span><br>fiber</td><td><span class="n">380</span><br>calories</td><td><span class="n">370 mg</span><br>sodium</td></tr></table>

## Chicken, barley and mushroom soup

*Sun's winter pot* &nbsp;·&nbsp; Serves 4 &nbsp;·&nbsp; 15 minutes hands-on, 45 minutes total

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

Barley has the kind of fiber that makes soup thick and your gut happy. Also Chang can't tell it's healthy, which is my favorite kind of recipe.
</div>

<table class="nut"><tr><td><span class="n">34 g</span><br>protein</td><td><span class="n">5.8 g</span><br>fiber</td><td><span class="n">320</span><br>calories</td><td><span class="n">420 mg</span><br>sodium</td></tr></table>

<p class="fine">Per serving. Calculated from USDA FoodData Central (E52); method and every ingredient value at the back of the book.</p>

### You need

- **1 1/2 cups** cooked pearled barley
- **8 oz** fresh shiitake mushrooms, sliced
- **2 medium** carrots, diced

- **1 medium** onion, diced
- **3** garlic cloves, minced

### Steps

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

## Korean radish and beef soup

*soegogi-muguk (Korean)* &nbsp;·&nbsp; Serves 4 &nbsp;·&nbsp; 15 minutes hands-on, 45 minutes total

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

Clear, clean, and the radish goes soft and sweet. When your stomach isn't sure about anything, it's sure about this.
</div>

<table class="nut"><tr><td><span class="n">23 g</span><br>protein</td><td><span class="n">3.8 g</span><br>fiber</td><td><span class="n">290</span><br>calories</td><td><span class="n">530 mg</span><br>sodium</td></tr></table>

<p class="fine">Per serving. Calculated from USDA FoodData Central (E52); method and every ingredient value at the back of the book.</p>

### You need

- **12 oz** lean beef chuck, in thin bite-size slices
- **1 lb** daikon radish, in thin squares
- **3** garlic cloves, minced
- **2 Tbsp** low-sodium soy sauce
- **1 Tbsp** toasted sesame oil
- **8 cups** water
- **3** scallions, sliced
- **1/4 tsp** salt
- **2 cups** cooked brown rice, to serve

### Steps

1. Heat the sesame oil in a pot. Cook the beef and garlic 3 minutes.
2. Add the radish and 1 Tbsp soy sauce. Stir 3 minutes.
3. Add the water. Boil, skim, then simmer 25 minutes until the radish is translucent.
4. Season with the rest of the soy sauce, then salt if needed. Scallions on top. Rice on the side.

**Soft-food version:** Cut the beef and radish very small; cook 10 minutes longer.

**Keeps:** Fridge 4 days, freezer 3 months.

</div>


<div class="recipe" markdown="1">

## Kimchi pancake with shrimp

*kimchi-jeon (Korean)* &nbsp;·&nbsp; Serves 3 &nbsp;·&nbsp; 15 minutes hands-on, 20 minutes total

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

The best use of kimchi that's gone sour. Whole-wheat flour, shrimp for protein. Rainy-day food. In California that's four days a year, so I make it when it's cloudy.
</div>

<table class="nut"><tr><td><span class="n">20 g</span><br>protein</td><td><span class="n">5.5 g</span><br>fiber</td><td><span class="n">300</span><br>calories</td><td><span class="n">340 mg</span><br>sodium</td></tr></table>

<p class="fine">Per serving. Calculated from USDA FoodData Central (E52); method and every ingredient value at the back of the book.</p>

### You need

- **1 cup** whole-wheat flour
- **1** large egg
- **1 cup + 2 Tbsp juice** sour kimchi, chopped
- **6 oz** raw shrimp, chopped
- **3** scallions, in 1-inch pieces
- **3/4 cup** cold water
- **2 Tbsp** canola oil

### Steps

1. Mix the flour, egg, kimchi and juice, and water into a thick batter. Fold in the shrimp and scallions.
2. Heat 1 Tbsp oil in a large nonstick skillet over medium heat. Spread half the batter thin.
3. Cook 4 minutes until the edges crisp, flip, and cook 4 more minutes until cooked through and the shrimp are opaque.
4. Repeat. Cut in squares.

**Soft-food version:** Make it thinner and cut it small; use soft white flour if whole-wheat is too coarse.

**Keeps:** Fridge 2 days. Re-crisp in a dry skillet until steaming.

<div class="box note" markdown="1">
<span class="label">Who should skip or ask first:</span> Kimchi is salty. Watching sodium? Small portions, or rinse it. Shellfish allergy: swap in cubed firm tofu, or chicken breast cooked to 165°F. High fiber. Go up slowly and drink water, or you'll feel it (E24).
</div>

</div>


<div class="recipe" markdown="1">

## Garlic eggplant with ground turkey

*mild yú xiāng qiézi (Chinese)* &nbsp;·&nbsp; Serves 4 &nbsp;·&nbsp; 25 minutes hands-on, 30 minutes total

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

Eggplant soaks up sauce like a sponge. I use turkey so it's lean. The name translates to 'fish-fragrant' but there's no fish. Don't ask me. Ask Sichuan.
</div>

<table class="nut"><tr><td><span class="n">30 g</span><br>protein</td><td><span class="n">7.9 g</span><br>fiber</td><td><span class="n">490</span><br>calories</td><td><span class="n">380 mg</span><br>sodium</td></tr></table>

<p class="fine">Per serving. Calculated from USDA FoodData Central (E52); method and every ingredient value at the back of the book.</p>

### You need

- **1 1/2 lb** eggplant (Chinese or globe), in finger-size strips
- **1 lb** ground turkey
- **3** garlic cloves, minced
- **1 Tbsp** minced ginger
- **3** scallions, sliced
- **2 Tbsp** low-sodium soy sauce
- **1 Tbsp** rice or white vinegar
- **1 tsp** sugar
- **1 Tbsp + 3 Tbsp water** cornstarch
- **2 Tbsp** canola oil
- **1 cup** low-sodium chicken broth
- **3 cups** cooked brown rice

### Steps

1. Heat 1 Tbsp oil in a large skillet. Add the eggplant and 1/4 cup water, cover, and cook 8 minutes, stirring once, until soft. Move to a bowl.
2. Add the remaining oil and the turkey. Cook, breaking it up, 6 to 8 minutes, until no pink remains (165°F).
3. Add garlic, ginger and most of the scallions. Stir 1 minute.
4. Return the eggplant. Add broth, soy sauce, vinegar and sugar. Simmer 3 minutes.
5. Stir in the cornstarch mixed with water until glossy. Top with scallions. Serve with rice.

**Soft-food version:** Peel the eggplant and cook it 5 minutes longer.

**Keeps:** Fridge 3 days.

<div class="box note" markdown="1">
<span class="label">Who should skip or ask first:</span> Kidney disease? Ask your doctor for your protein number (E28). High fiber. Go up slowly and drink water, or you'll feel it (E24).
</div>

</div>


<div class="recipe" markdown="1">

## Hand-torn cabbage with pork

*shǒu sī bāo cài (Chinese)* &nbsp;·&nbsp; Serves 3 &nbsp;·&nbsp; 15 minutes hands-on, 20 minutes total

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

You tear the cabbage with your hands. Good for grip, good for dinner. Chang says it's his 'grip program'. It's not. It's cabbage.
</div>

<table class="nut"><tr><td><span class="n">30 g</span><br>protein</td><td><span class="n">5.5 g</span><br>fiber</td><td><span class="n">370</span><br>calories</td><td><span class="n">280 mg</span><br>sodium</td></tr></table>

<p class="fine">Per serving. Calculated from USDA FoodData Central (E52); method and every ingredient value at the back of the book.</p>

### You need

- **1 lb** green cabbage, torn into pieces
- **12 oz** pork loin, thinly sliced
- **3** garlic cloves, sliced
- **1 Tbsp** low-sodium soy sauce
- **1 Tbsp** rice or white vinegar
- **1/2 tsp** sugar
- **1 Tbsp** canola oil
- **1/2 tsp** red pepper flakes (optional)
- **1 1/2 cups** cooked brown rice

### Steps

1. Heat the oil in a wok or large skillet over high heat. Cook the pork 3 to 4 minutes, until no pink remains (145°F). Move to a plate.
2. Add garlic and pepper flakes for 20 seconds, then the cabbage. Stir-fry 4 to 5 minutes until wilted with some crisp edges.
3. Return the pork. Add soy sauce, vinegar and sugar. Toss 1 minute. Serve with rice.

**Soft-food version:** Cut the cabbage in small pieces and cook it 3 minutes longer, covered.

**Keeps:** Fridge 3 days.

<div class="box note" markdown="1">
<span class="label">Who should skip or ask first:</span> Kidney disease? Ask your doctor for your protein number (E28). High fiber. Go up slowly and drink water, or you'll feel it (E24).
</div>

*Sun's summer bowl* &nbsp;·&nbsp; Serves 2 &nbsp;·&nbsp; 10 minutes hands-on, 10 minutes total

<div class="sun" markdown="1">

<p class="fine">Per serving. Calculated from USDA FoodData Central (E52); method and every ingredient value at the back of the book.</p>

- **1** scallion, sliced
- **1 Tbsp** rice or white vinegar
- **1 tsp** toasted sesame oil

- **1 tsp** toasted sesame seeds

### Steps

1. Whisk the vinegar, sesame oil and soy sauce in a bowl.
2. Add the edamame, corn, cucumber, tofu and scallion. Toss.

## Beef and vegetable glass noodles, lighter

*japchae (Korean)* &nbsp;·&nbsp; Serves 4 &nbsp;·&nbsp; 35 minutes hands-on, 40 minutes total

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

Japchae is party food. I made it Tuesday food: more vegetables, more beef, fewer noodles. Nobody at the party complained.
</div>

<table class="nut"><tr><td><span class="n">26 g</span><br>protein</td><td><span class="n">4.0 g</span><br>fiber</td><td><span class="n">400</span><br>calories</td><td><span class="n">570 mg</span><br>sodium</td></tr></table>

<p class="fine">Per serving. Calculated from USDA FoodData Central (E52); method and every ingredient value at the back of the book.</p>

### You need

- **4 oz dry** sweet potato glass noodles (dangmyeon)
- **12 oz** top sirloin, in thin strips
- **5 oz** fresh spinach
- **2 medium** carrots, in matchsticks
- **1 medium** onion, sliced
- **4 oz** fresh shiitake mushrooms, sliced
- **1 medium** red bell pepper, in strips
- **2** large eggs (thin omelet, cooked firm)
- **3 Tbsp** low-sodium soy sauce
- **1 Tbsp** honey
- **1 Tbsp** toasted sesame oil
- **1 Tbsp** canola oil
- **3** garlic cloves, grated
- **1 Tbsp** toasted sesame seeds

### Steps

1. Cook the noodles in boiling water 6 minutes, drain, rinse, and cut with scissors into shorter lengths.
2. Blanch the spinach 30 seconds, rinse cold, squeeze dry.
3. Beat the eggs and cook as a thin omelet in a nonstick pan until fully set. Roll and slice into strips.
4. Stir-fry the beef in half the oil until no pink remains. Remove. Stir-fry the onion, carrots, mushrooms and pepper in the rest, 4 minutes.
5. Mix soy sauce, honey, sesame oil and garlic. Toss everything together with the sauce. Top with sesame seeds.

**Soft-food version:** Cut the noodles and vegetables short and cook the vegetables 2 minutes longer.

**Keeps:** Fridge 3 days. Eat at room temperature or warm gently.

<div class="box note" markdown="1">
<span class="label">Who should skip or ask first:</span> On warfarin? Keep greens steady from week to week; don't suddenly change how much you eat. Ask your doctor. Honey: never for babies under 1. Diabetes: honey counts as sugar (or leave it out). Kidney disease? Ask your doctor for your protein number (E28).
</div>

</div>

## Cold soy-milk noodle soup

*kongguksu (Korean)* &nbsp;·&nbsp; Serves 2 &nbsp;·&nbsp; 15 minutes hands-on, 20 minutes total

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

The summer noodle. Cold, creamy, nutty. Traditionally you grind soaked soybeans; this shortcut uses soy milk and tofu. My mother would call it lazy. My knees call it smart.

<table class="nut"><tr><td><span class="n">34 g</span><br>protein</td><td><span class="n">9.0 g</span><br>fiber</td><td><span class="n">520</span><br>calories</td><td><span class="n">800 mg</span><br>sodium</td></tr></table>

- **1/2 medium** cucumber, in matchsticks

### Steps

1. Blend the soy milk, tofu, sesame seeds and salt until smooth. Chill.
2. Cook the noodles, then rinse under cold water until cold.
3. Divide noodles into bowls, pour the cold soy broth over, top with cucumber and a hard-boiled egg (boiled 10 minutes, yolk firm).

<div class="box note" markdown="1">

This one is on the salty side (about 800 mg sodium per serving). Watching sodium? Use half the paste or soy sauce and add water or unsalted broth.
</div>

*fānqié dòufu dàn huā tāng (Chinese)* &nbsp;·&nbsp; Serves 4 &nbsp;·&nbsp; 10 minutes hands-on, 25 minutes total

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

Sweet-sour broth, soft tofu, egg ribbons. When a grandchild is sick, I make this. When I'm tired, Chang makes this. He's getting better at it. Seven out of ten.

### You need

- **4 medium** tomatoes, in wedges
- **1 block (14 oz)** firm tofu, in cubes

### Steps

1. Heat the oil in a pot. Cook the tomatoes 5 minutes, pressing them, until saucy.
2. Add broth, water, sugar and salt. Simmer 8 minutes.
3. Add tofu and peas. Simmer 3 minutes.
4. Stir the soup in a circle and drizzle in the eggs. Simmer 1 minute more so the egg is fully cooked. Top with scallions.

## Gochujang chicken with sweet potato and broccoli

*Sun's sheet-pan dinner* &nbsp;·&nbsp; Serves 4 &nbsp;·&nbsp; 15 minutes hands-on, 45 minutes total

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

One pan. You chop, you toss, you sit down. Forty-five minutes later dinner happens. This is how women my age should cook on weeknights: sitting down.
</div>

<table class="nut"><tr><td><span class="n">39 g</span><br>protein</td><td><span class="n">5.8 g</span><br>fiber</td><td><span class="n">390</span><br>calories</td><td><span class="n">630 mg</span><br>sodium</td></tr></table>

<p class="fine">Per serving. Calculated from USDA FoodData Central (E52); method and every ingredient value at the back of the book.</p>

### You need

- **1 1/2 lb** boneless, skinless chicken thighs, in large pieces
- **2 medium** sweet potatoes, in 1-inch cubes
- **1 lb** broccoli florets

- **2 Tbsp** gochujang
- **1 Tbsp** honey
- **1 Tbsp** low-sodium soy sauce

### Steps

2. Mix gochujang, honey, soy sauce, oil and garlic. Toss the chicken in half; toss the sweet potato and onion in the rest.

**Soft-food version:** Cut everything small and roast the sweet potato 10 minutes longer.

**Keeps:** Fridge 3 days. Reheat to 165°F.

<div class="box note" markdown="1">
<span class="label">Who should skip or ask first:</span> Kidney disease? Ask your doctor for your protein number (E28). High fiber. Go up slowly and drink water, or you'll feel it (E24). Honey: never for babies under 1. Diabetes: honey counts as sugar (or leave it out). On warfarin? Keep greens steady from week to week; don't suddenly change how much you eat. Ask your doctor.
</div>

</div>

# The Sunday kitchen lessons

Twelve short lessons with Sun. Full scripts; the same content is in programs.json.


# GUT-W01 · Count what you eat now

| Type | Length | Set | Wardrobe | Voices |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gut Reset kitchen lesson | 5:45 | SET-KITCHEN | S-KITCHEN | Sun |

<div class="box note" markdown="1">

# How we calculated the recipe numbers

**Source.** Every ingredient is matched to a food in the USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy database (April 2018 release, downloaded from fdc.nal.usda.gov, E52). We took energy (kcal), protein, total dietary fiber and sodium per 100 grams, multiplied by the grams used, added up the recipe and divided by the number of servings.

**Two pastes aren't in the USDA database:** gochujang and chunjang. For those we used the manufacturer label values recorded on Open Food Facts (Sempio gochujang, Obok chunjang, E53). The chunjang label's protein (20 g per 100 g) looks high for a bean paste, so treat the protein in Chang's black bean noodles as a slight overestimate (the paste adds about 3.6 g per serving).

**Rules we followed.**

- Meat, fish and tofu are weighed **raw**, matched to raw USDA values. Rice and pasta are weighed **cooked**, matched to cooked values (1 cup cooked brown rice = 195 g; 1 cup cooked whole-wheat pasta = 140 g).
- Salt, soy sauce and pastes are counted in full at the amounts listed. "Pinch" and "to taste" items, and water, count as zero.
- Dried wakame is calculated as its soaked weight (1/2 oz dry ≈ 140 g soaked) using USDA raw wakame.
- Where USDA reports no value for a nutrient (fiber in raw shrimp and short-grain white rice), we counted zero. Shrimp has essentially no fiber; white rice has a little, so those fiber numbers are slightly low.
- Soy-braised eggs: all the soy sauce is counted even though most stays in the pot, so sodium is overstated.
- Brand, ripeness and exact size change real numbers. Treat these as good estimates, within about 10%.

Numbers are rounded: protein to the nearest gram, fiber to 0.1 g, calories and sodium to the nearest 10.

# Where the numbers come from

Every number and health statement in this book traces to one of the entries below. They are the same evidence IDs our whole team uses (EVIDENCE.md). Grade A means a Cochrane review, a large meta-analysis or a guideline body. B means a single good trial or a small meta-analysis. C means an observational study: it shows a link, not cause and effect. D means lab, physiology or label data.


<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E23** (grade A− (meta)). Light walking after meals (even 2–5 minutes) lowers the post-meal glucose rise compared with sitting.

<p class="src">Source: Buffey et al., Sports Med 2022 — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35147898/</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E24** (grade A (meta of cohorts + RCTs)). Fiber: 25–29 g/day was linked with 15–30% lower all-cause and CV mortality, type 2 diabetes and colorectal cancer. More fiber was linked with more benefit.

<p class="src">Source: Reynolds et al., Lancet 2019 — https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(18)31809-9/fulltext</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E25** (grade B (exploratory)). Chronic constipation: 2 green kiwifruit/day vs 100 g prunes vs 12 g psyllium, 4 weeks, 75 patients. All three improved bowel movements similarly. Kiwi had the fewest side effects and highest satisfaction, and improved bloating.

<p class="src">Source: Chey et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2021 — https://www.healio.com/news/gastroenterology/20210608/kiwi-fruit-effectively-relieves-symptoms-in-chronic-constipation</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E26** (grade B (small)). 36 adults, 10 weeks. A high-fermented-food diet (yogurt, kefir, kimchi, sauerkraut, kombucha; intake rose to about 6 servings/day by the end) increased microbiome diversity and lowered 19 inflammatory proteins (including IL-6). The high-fiber arm didn't show those changes over 10 weeks.

<p class="src">Source: Wastyk et al., Cell 2021 — https://med.stanford.edu/news/all-news/2021/07/fermented-food-diet-increases-microbiome-diversity-lowers-inflammation.html</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E27** (grade B). Prune Study: postmenopausal women eating 50 g prunes/day (about 5–6) preserved total hip BMD over 12 months vs controls.

<p class="src">Source: De Souza et al., Am J Clin Nutr 2022 — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9193411/</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E28** (grade A (consensus)). PROT-AGE: adults over 65 should get 1.0–1.2 g protein/kg/day, and 1.2–1.5 g/kg if active or ill (unless there is severe kidney disease). Aim for 25–30 g per meal with about 2.5–2.8 g leucine.

<p class="src">Source: Bauer et al., JAMDA 2013 — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23867520/</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E32** (grade A−). Honey improved upper-respiratory-infection symptoms, especially cough frequency and severity, compared with usual care. Never give honey to infants under 12 months.

<p class="src">Source: Abuelgasim et al., BMJ Evid Based Med 2021 — https://www.phc.ox.ac.uk/news/honey-better-than-usual-care-for-easing-respiratory-symptoms-especially-cough</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E33** (grade A−). Ginger for osteoarthritis pain: small effect vs placebo, with more GI complaints. Say it "may help a little". Ginger for nausea has reasonable support. It can interact with blood thinners at supplement doses.

<p class="src">Source: Bartels et al., Osteoarthritis Cartilage 2015 — https://www.oarsijournal.com/article/S1063-4584(14)00641-4/fulltext ; ginger umbrella review AJCN 2022 — https://ajcn.nutrition.org/article/S0002-9165(22)00277-5/fulltext</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E35** (grade B+). Salt substitute (25% potassium chloride) in 20,995 older adults at high risk: stroke, major CV events and death were all reduced. Caution: potassium salt isn't for people with kidney disease or on potassium-raising medicines. Always say "ask your doctor first".

<p class="src">Source: Neal et al., NEJM 2021 (SSaSS) — https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2105675</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E52** (grade A (reference database)). USDA FoodData Central, SR Legacy (April 2018 release): per-100 g energy, protein, total dietary fiber, sodium and leucine used for every recipe calculation in Sun Yoon's Strong Kitchen (FDC IDs listed per ingredient in the book's method appendix).

<p class="src">Source: Opened/downloaded https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/fdc-datasets/FoodData_Central_sr_legacy_food_csv_2018-04.zip</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E53** (grade D (label data)). Label values for two Korean pastes not in SR Legacy, per 100 g: Sempio gochujang (barcode 8801005000178) 233 kcal, 5.0 g protein, 2.7 g fiber, 2,640 mg sodium; Obok chunjang (8801126032447) 200 kcal, 20 g protein, 0 g fiber, 3,200 mg sodium (single crowd-sourced label; protein looks high, so treat as approximate).

<p class="src">Source: Open Food Facts API — opened https://world.openfoodfacts.org/product/8801005000178 , https://world.openfoodfacts.org/product/8801126032447</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E54** (grade A (federal guidance)). Safe minimum internal temperatures: ground meat 160°F; beef/pork steaks, chops, roasts 145°F + 3-minute rest; all poultry 165°F; fish 145°F or until opaque and flaking; shrimp until pearly/opaque; clams until shells open; eggs until yolk and white are firm; egg dishes 160°F; leftovers 165°F.

<p class="src">Source: FoodSafety.gov — opened https://www.foodsafety.gov/food-safety-charts/safe-minimum-internal-temperatures</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E55** (grade A (federal guidance)). Adults 65+ are at higher risk of foodborne illness (weaker immune response, slower gut transit, less stomach acid, reduced liver and kidney clearance).

<p class="src">Source: FoodSafety.gov — opened https://www.foodsafety.gov/people-at-risk/older-adults</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E58** (grade A (NIH fact sheet)). Seaweed iodine varies enormously: commercially available seaweeds measured 16 to 2,984 mcg iodine per gram. Adult upper limit 1,100 mcg/day from all sources. People with autoimmune thyroid disease may have adverse effects at intakes considered safe for others.

<p class="src">Source: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements — opened https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Iodine-HealthProfessional/ , https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Iodine-Consumer/</p>

</div>
